title: Date and Time
description: The modern java.time API: LocalDate, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, Duration, Period, and formatting/parsing.
objectives: Create and manipulate LocalDate, LocalTime, and LocalDateTime
Format and parse dates/times with DateTimeFormatter

content.heading: LocalDate, LocalTime, and LocalDateTime
content.body: Since Java 8, java.time is the standard, immutable, thread-safe date/time API, replacing the older, mutable and famously error-prone java.util.Date/Calendar. LocalDate represents a date with no time component (2024-03-15); LocalTime represents a time with no date (14:30:00); LocalDateTime combines both. All are immutable — methods like plusDays(n) or minusHours(n) return a new instance rather than modifying the original, exactly like String's immutability model. LocalDate.now()/LocalTime.now()/LocalDateTime.now() capture the current value from the system clock.

content.heading: Duration, Period, and Formatting
content.body:
Duration measures a time-based amount (hours, minutes, seconds — appropriate between two LocalTime or LocalDateTime instants): Duration.between(start, end). Period measures a date-based amount (years, months, days — appropriate between two LocalDate values): Period.between(startDate, endDate). Using the wrong one for the wrong context (e.g., Period for elapsed seconds) doesn't fit the data conceptually, since months/years don't have a fixed length in seconds the way Duration expects.

DateTimeFormatter controls how these types convert to and from text: date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/yyyy")) produces a formatted string; LocalDate.parse(text, formatter) does the reverse, parsing text back into a LocalDate (throwing DateTimeParseException for malformed input).

content.explanation: plusDays(7) returns a new LocalDate rather than mutating today. Period.between measures the date-based gap in years/months/days; DateTimeFormatter converts a LocalDate to a custom text format.

keyPoints: java.time (LocalDate/LocalTime/LocalDateTime) is immutable and the modern standard, replacing Date/Calendar
Duration measures time-based amounts (hours/minutes/seconds); Period measures date-based amounts (years/months/days)
DateTimeFormatter handles both formatting (date -> text) and parsing (text -> date)
All java.time manipulation methods (plusDays, minusHours, ...) return new instances
commonMistakes: Using the legacy Date/Calendar classes in new code instead of java.time
Using Period where Duration was needed (or vice versa) for the kind of quantity being measured
Not catching DateTimeParseException when parsing text that might not match the expected format
